context: Exactly one queen must occupy each row. The backtracking algorithm places queens in rows 1 through 4 in order, preventing row conflicts. At each level, try columns 1 through 4 in order and prune any branch where the new queen shares a column or diagonal with a queen already on the board. Row and column numbers start at 1.
description: The figure expands only the branch that chooses column 2 in the first row. In the next three rows it keeps columns 4, 1, and 3, respectively. Ellipses after columns 1, 3, and 4 of the first row mean their continuations are omitted, not that those branches are pruned. Column 3 in the first row leads to another valid solution, [3, 1, 4, 2].

The table gives the decision for each candidate square. If a square conflicts with several queens, the figure and table identify just one conflict, which is enough to prune the branch. For example, the figure shows (4,2) sharing a main diagonal with (3,1). It also shares a column with (1,2) and the other diagonal with (2,4). “Valid” in the table means only that the current move causes no conflict. The branch may still fail to yield a solution.

frames.explanation: A grayed-out candidate with a pruning mark violates a constraint. An ellipsis on a valid first-row branch simply leaves its continuation out of the drawing.
frames.title: Trying squares row by row and pruning conflicting placements

summary: The branch that places the first queen in column 2 illustrates how the search tries and prunes 16 candidate boards over four levels. The chosen columns, in row order, form the valid solution [2, 4, 1, 3].
